extracted.intended_audience: citizens of New York / voters and readers engaged in the 1787–88 constitutional ratification debate; general public interested in constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and standards for designing and assessing the national Executive (the President) in a republican constitution, focusing on the balance between executive energy and republican safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified veto / return-and-reconsider power
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power to return a bill, which shall have passed the two branches of the legislature, for reconsideration; and the bill so returned is to become a law, if, upon that reconsideration, it be approved by two thirds of both houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with the British sovereign's absolute negative. The Federalist emphasizes that a qualified negative (a return-for-reconsideration subject to legislative override) is very different in kind and safer than an absolute veto; historical disuse of an absolute negative does not negate its existence. The comparison to state councils of revision (shared veto-like power) is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of commander-in-chief authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to be the 'commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States, when called into the actual service of the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This command is 'occasional' regarding state militias and is therefore more limited than the always-entire command of militias by some state governors or the British king. The President's role is supreme command and direction of military and naval forces, but the power to declare war and to raise/regulate fleets and armies belongs to the legislature under the proposed Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The President will have power to grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, EXCEPT IN CASES OF IMPEACHMENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts this limitation with broader gubernatorial pardon powers (e.g., New York's governor may pardon in all cases except treason and murder) and argues that excluding impeachment from the pardon power prevents the executive from shielding participants in conspiracies against government via pre-emptive pardons; impeachment remains a political check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to recommend, convene, and adjourn the legislature (limited adjournment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may recommend to Congress measures he deems necessary; convene, on extraordinary occasions, both houses or either of them; and, in case of disagreement between them WITH RESPECT TO THE TIME OF ADJOURNMENT, adjourn them to such time as he shall think proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convening is framed as a matter of administrative convenience (avoiding constant legislative convocations). The adjournment power is narrowly defined (only for disagreement on time), distinct from the British monarch's ability to prorogue or dissolve Parliament and from broader state governor powers to prorogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making with Senate advice and consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constitutional arrangement gives the federal Executive a treaty power subject to a legislative check, contrasted with the British king's effective sole prerogative in treaty-making; the paper notes that because treaties affect national sovereignty, the federal Executive's authority here naturally exceeds that of state executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception of ambassadors as dignity and administrative convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is also to be authorized to receive ambassadors and other public ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats this mainly as a matter of dignity rather than substantive authority; arranging reception by the Executive avoids having to convene the legislature for routine arrivals of foreign ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointments by nomination with Senate advice-and-consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to nominate, and, WITH THE ADVICE AND CONSENT OF THE SENATE, to appoint ambassadors and other public ministers, judges of the Supreme Court, and in general all officers of the United States established by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison to British royal appointment powers and to state appointment practices (e.g., New York governor + council) highlights how publicity and a larger Senate make influence more difficult than small secret councils. If the Senate is divided, appointments cannot be made, whereas some state executives could decide by casting vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy in the Executive as a normative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition of good government — essential for protection against foreign attacks, steady administration of the laws, protection of property, and security of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay positions 'energy' as the chief positive quality to seek in an Executive, arguing that a feeble Executive implies feeble execution and therefore bad government in practice. Energy must be balanced with republican safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of executive energy: unity, duration, adequate provision for support, competent powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are, first, unity; secondly, duration; thirdly, an adequate provision for its support; fourthly, competent powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each ingredient is necessary: unity promotes decision and dispatch; duration supplies stability of conduct; adequate support (salary, independence) prevents dependence on transient interests; competent powers ensure the Executive can execute laws effectively. These must be combined with safety ingredients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the Executive (single magistrate vs plurality or council)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity is conducive to energy — decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch characterize the proceedings of one man more than of a number; unity may be destroyed by vesting power in two or more magistrates or by subjecting an ostensible Executive to the control of counsellors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay gives historical and reasoned objections to plurality: disagreements, personal emulation, factionalism, impeded measures, weakened authority, and danger in times of crisis (e.g., war). It criticizes executive councils as sources of collusion and as cloaks for faults; unity also makes the Executive a single object for public jealousy and watchfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety in a republican Executive: due dependence on the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute safety in the republican sense are, first, a due dependence on the people...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependence on the people provides democratic checks — the Executive must be responsive to public opinion and structures that enable popular control, balancing energy with accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety in a republican Executive: due responsibility (censure and punishment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute safety in the republican sense are... secondly, a due responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility includes censure (public opinion) and legal punishment; it is especially important in elective offices because officials are more likely to act in ways that merit loss of trust than to incur legal penalties. A single Executive makes responsibility clearer and enforcement easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality undermines responsibility and obscures blame
rubrics_metrics.description: A little plurality often tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility; when multiple actors exist, 'it often becomes impossible... to determine on whom the blame or the punishment... ought really to fall.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay uses the example of the governor plus council and the council of appointment to show how mutual accusations and divided responsibility prevent the public from identifying and punishing malfeasance; plurality invites pretexts like 'I was overruled by my council.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality requires large numbers to be secure but increases expense and inefficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: To render plurality secure against combination, numbers must be so great as to render combination difficult; but such numbers carry prohibitive public expense and practical drawbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small councils are easy to influence or to combine; large numbers are costly and impractical. The essay warns that councils (even moderate-sized ones) can be instruments or accomplices of vice and a cloak for faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive should be electable for a fixed term and personally accountable (non-hereditary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President of the United States would be an officer elected by the people for FOUR years; the king of Great Britain is a perpetual and HEREDITARY prince. The one would be amenable to personal punishment and disgrace; the person of the other is sacred and inviolable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed-term, elective character ensures that the Executive is subject to public scrutiny and accountability, unlike hereditary monarchs who are immune; this supports republican safety while allowing executive energy.
